Sole Smart Actions: Understanding What a Wallet User Wants¶

Sole is a digital wallet. Today, a user who wants to send money, pay a bill or check a group's contributions has to know where in the app that action lives — which menu, which tab, which screen. Users do not think in menu labels. They think in goals: "send 50 to Litia", "pay my electricity", "how much is in my wallet?". Every extra screen is friction, and friction falls hardest on the users with the least digital experience.

Sole Smart Actions is a natural-language entry point: the user types a short command, and the app opens the right workflow. The heart of it is an intent classifier — a model that reads the command and predicts which of eight supported actions the user wants. The model only routes: it never executes a payment. The user always confirms the details on the screen the model opens.

The task looks easy, and mostly it is. The difficulty is concentrated in a few places that matter a lot. Consider four commands from the data we are about to use:

  • "Send 60 fiji dollars to litia" → TRANSFER_MONEY
  • "Transfer failed" → HELP_SUPPORT
  • "Cash withdrawal 120" → WITHDRAW_MONEY
  • "Show withdrawals this week" → VIEW_TRANSACTIONS

The word transfer appears in a command that should open the transfer screen and in one that should open help. The word withdrawal appears in a request to take cash out and in a request to look at past withdrawals. A model that only counts words sees the same signal in both; telling them apart requires reading how the words relate to each other.

And two kinds of mistakes are not equal. Opening the balance screen for someone who wanted their transaction history costs a tap. Opening a money-moving workflow — a transfer, a withdrawal, a bill payment — for someone who wanted something else is a different matter. There is a third kind of mistake too: users will type things the app cannot do ("tell me a joke", "book a cinema"). The model must recognise that it does not know, and fall back to help instead of guessing.

Roadmap. One model, a fine-tuned pre-trained Transformer, competes against two benchmarks:

Section Model Hyperparameters chosen on validation
2 Benchmarks: majority class and a hand-written keyword rule keywords per intent
4 Fine-tuned DistilBERT (Section 3 explains the pre-trained model it starts from) how much to unfreeze, learning rate, epochs

Each model section ends with a Final configuration cell, scores that configuration once on the test set, and adds it to a running summary table that accumulates every final model so far, as in Lecture 12. Test scores are reported, never used to choose: hyperparameters, thresholds and the deployment decision are all made on validation. As in Lecture 12, once a model's hyperparameters are chosen it is refit on training + validation before it is scored on test. Section 5 puts a confidence gate on each final model (calibrated confidences, threshold chosen for business value). Section 6 compares the final models after the gate and recommends which model to deploy.

Setup¶

We locate the repository, set up the folder for figures, and import the packages used throughout. As in Lecture 12, we use scikit-learn for the metrics and Hugging Face transformers on PyTorch for the pre-trained model.

1. The Sole Smart Actions dataset¶

The dataset contains 3,000 short commands that a wallet user might type, each labelled with the action it should trigger.

  • Industry: digital financial services (mobile wallet)
  • Target variable: intent — one of eight supported actions (plus an optional ninth, CHECK_SPENDING)
  • Feature variable: the raw text of the command — nothing else
  • Unsupported requests: 300 commands labelled UNKNOWN_INTENT, which the app cannot serve. They are not a class the model learns: they exist only to test whether the model knows when to say "I don't know".

Two properties of the data shape everything that follows. First, the utterances are synthetic: generated from templates, then cleaned. They are shorter and more regular than what real users type. Second, the dataset ships with its own split — train, validation, test and evaluation_only — and its README spells out the protocol: train on train, tune models and the rejection threshold on validation, and score once on test. We follow it, with one addition taken from Lectures 10–12: we remove duplicate commands, so that the same text can never appear in two subsets. When a command appears in several subsets, we keep the training copy.

Training, validation and test sets¶

We encode each supported intent as an integer 0–7 and give unsupported commands the label -1.

The unsupported commands need one more decision. The dataset README warns that if we use them to tune the rejection threshold, they are no longer an untouched test set. So we split them in half, at random: half to tune the threshold, together with the validation set, and half held out to measure the fallback once at the very end, together with the test set.

In [6]:
def make_splits(data):
    """Integer labels and the indices of each subset, following the dataset's own split."""
    labels = np.array([CLASSES.index(i) if i in CLASSES else -1 for i in data["intent"]])
    split = data["split"].values
    train = np.where((split == "train") & (labels >= 0))[0]
    val = np.where((split == "validation") & (labels >= 0))[0]
    test = np.where((split == "test") & (labels >= 0))[0]

    # Unsupported commands: half to tune the threshold, half held out
    unknown = np.where(labels == -1)[0]
    shuffled = np.random.RandomState(SEED).permutation(unknown)
    unk_tune = np.sort(shuffled[: len(unknown) // 2])
    unk_hold = np.sort(shuffled[len(unknown) // 2:])
    return labels, data["text"].values, train, val, test, unknown, unk_tune, unk_hold


def describe_splits():
    """Size of each subset and the share of each intent in it."""
    print(f"Training set:          {len(train_idx):,} commands")
    print(f"Validation set:        {len(val_idx):,} commands  + {len(unk_tune_idx)} unsupported (threshold tuning)")
    print(f"Test set:              {len(test_idx):,} commands  + {len(unk_hold_idx)} unsupported (held out)")
    split_check = pd.DataFrame({
        "Training": pd.Series(y[train_idx]).value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().values,
        "Validation": pd.Series(y[val_idx]).value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().values,
        "Test": pd.Series(y[test_idx]).value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().values,
    }, index=CLASSES)
    display(split_check.style.format("{:.1%}").set_caption("Class shares by subset"))


y, texts, train_idx, val_idx, test_idx, unknown_idx, unk_tune_idx, unk_hold_idx = make_splits(dat)

# The two evaluation pools for the confidence gate of Section 5
gate_val_idx = np.concatenate([val_idx, unk_tune_idx])
gate_test_idx = np.concatenate([test_idx, unk_hold_idx])

describe_splits()

Command length in words: median 5, 95th percentile 9, maximum 12

Three observations.

The commands are very short — five words at the median. There is little context to work with, so single words carry most of the signal: send, pay, withdraw, balance, group.

Several intents share vocabulary. HELP_SUPPORT is full of words from other intents ("transfer failed", "reset my pin"); VIEW_TRANSACTIONS talks about withdrawals and payments; CHECK_BALANCE mentions amounts, like TRANSFER_MONEY and WITHDRAW_MONEY.

The commands carry local flavor: Fijian names (Litia, Savenaca, Roshni), Fiji dollars, agents, church and market-vendor savings groups. A model trained on generic English has never seen most of these names.

Duplicates and leakage¶

Template-generated data repeats itself. If the same command appears in the training and the test set, the test set rewards memorization. We check how often that happens.

In [8]:
normalized = dat["text"].str.lower().str.strip()
train_texts_seen = set(normalized.iloc[train_idx])

seen_in_train = normalized.isin(train_texts_seen).values
test_unseen_idx = test_idx[~seen_in_train[test_idx]]

print(f"Exact duplicate commands in the working sample: {normalized.duplicated().sum():,}")
print(f"Validation commands also in training:           {seen_in_train[val_idx].sum()} / {len(val_idx)}")
print(f"Test commands also in training:                 {seen_in_train[test_idx].sum()} / {len(test_idx)}")

This version of the data has no duplicates, within or across subsets. We keep the removal step anyway, as in Lectures 10–12, so that the protocol still holds if the data changes.

Removing duplicates¶

Lectures 10–12 drop exact duplicates before splitting, so that identical text cannot appear in two subsets and flatter the out-of-sample estimate. Our split comes with the dataset, so we keep one copy of each command — the training copy when there is one — and rebuild the subsets on the deduplicated data. Here nothing is removed, so every subset stays perfectly balanced (12.5% per intent); the results still report macro F1.

In [9]:
SPLIT_PRIORITY = {"train": 0, "validation": 1, "test": 2, "evaluation_only": 3}

before = len(dat)
dat = (
    dat.assign(key=lambda d: d["text"].str.lower().str.strip(),
               priority=lambda d: d["split"].map(SPLIT_PRIORITY))
       .sort_values("priority", kind="stable")       # the training copy comes first
       .drop_duplicates(subset="key")                # no command in two subsets
       .sort_index()
       .drop(columns=["key", "priority"])
       .reset_index(drop=True)
)
print(f"Duplicates removed: {before - len(dat):,}  ->  working sample: {len(dat):,} commands")
display(
    pd.crosstab(dat["intent"], dat["split"], margins=True, margins_name="Total")
      .reindex(CLASSES + [UNKNOWN, "Total"])
      [["train", "validation", "test", "evaluation_only", "Total"]]
)

# Rebuild the subsets on the deduplicated data
y, texts, train_idx, val_idx, test_idx, unknown_idx, unk_tune_idx, unk_hold_idx = make_splits(dat)
gate_val_idx = np.concatenate([val_idx, unk_tune_idx])
gate_test_idx = np.concatenate([test_idx, unk_hold_idx])

# Check: no command left in two subsets

test_unseen_idx = test_idx[~seen_in_train[test_idx]]

Word lift¶

Which words identify each intent? As in Lecture 11, for each word and intent we compare how often the word appears in that intent to how often it appears everywhere else, using the training set only:

$$\text{lift}(\text{word}, \text{intent}) = \frac{\text{rate of the word within the intent}}{\text{rate of the word outside the intent}}$$

In [10]:
def simple_words(text):
    """Minimal cleaning used for exploration only: lowercase, strip punctuation, split."""
    return re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", text.lower()).split()


def distinctive_words(texts_subset, labels_subset, category, min_count=8, top_n=10, smoothing=1.0):
    """Rank words by how much more often they appear in one intent than elsewhere."""
    in_class = Counter(w for t, l in zip(texts_subset, labels_subset) if l == category
                       for w in simple_words(t))
    out_class = Counter(w for t, l in zip(texts_subset, labels_subset) if l != category
                        for w in simple_words(t))
    n_in, n_out = sum(in_class.values()), sum(out_class.values())

    rows = []
    for word, count in in_class.items():
        if not word.isalpha() or len(word) < 3 or count + out_class[word] < min_count:
            continue
        rate_in = (count + smoothing) / n_in
        rate_out = (out_class[word] + smoothing) / n_out
        rows.append((word, rate_in / rate_out, count))

    return (
        pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["word", "lift", "count"])
        .sort_values("lift", ascending=False)
        .head(top_n)
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )


train_labels = [CLASSES[k] for k in y[train_idx]]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(22, 10))
for ax, intent in zip(axes.ravel(), CLASSES):
    top = distinctive_words(texts[train_idx], train_labels, intent).iloc[::-1]
    ax.barh(top["word"], top["lift"], color=CLASS_COLORS[intent], edgecolor="white")
    ax.axvline(1, color=INK, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_title(intent, fontsize=FONTSIZE)
    ax.set_xlabel("Lift (log scale)", fontsize=FONTSIZE - 2)
    ax.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

plt.tight_layout()
save_figure(fig, "01_word_lift")
plt.show()

Most intents have a handful of words with enormous lifts — send and transfer for transfers, bill and pay for bill payment, group and contributed for groups. A model that knows which words appear will get a long way. The interesting cases are the words that also appear in other intents, which is where Section 6 will find the errors.

2. Evaluation protocol and two benchmarks¶

One protocol for every model. Each model is fitted on the training set, and its hyperparameters are chosen on the validation set. Each model section shows every configuration tried, the validation results, and a Final configuration cell that states what was chosen and why. Once a model's final configuration is fixed, it is scored once on the test set at the end of its section and added to a running summary table with every final model before it. Test scores are reported for comparison, never used to choose anything.

Refit on training + validation. As in Lecture 12, once the hyperparameters are chosen, the final configuration is refit on training + validation with those hyperparameters (and, for neural networks, the number of epochs chosen by early stopping), and it is this refit model that is scored on test and deployed. We keep both versions of each model: the version fitted on training alone gives honest validation predictions, which Section 5 uses to calibrate confidences and choose thresholds; the refit version gives the test predictions. The threshold chosen on the first is applied unchanged to the second, as Lecture 12 does with its confidence cutoff.

Selection rule. The configuration with the highest validation accuracy wins. The validation set has 240 commands, so one command is worth about 0.4 points of accuracy and ties are common. Ties go to the configuration with the lower validation log loss: among equally accurate models, the one whose probabilities are more trustworthy, which is what the confidence gate relies on.

Every model produces a probability for each of the eight intents, for every command — including the unsupported ones — so that Section 5 can put a confidence gate on any of them. Beyond accuracy we record the number of parameters and the latency of answering one command end to end, the deck's "practical deployment" criteria.

In [11]:
ABSTAIN = -2        # a prediction meaning "no intent chosen": the keyword rule can abstain
REFIT_IDX = np.concatenate([train_idx, val_idx])     # training + validation, for the final refit
FINALISTS = {}      # model name -> final configuration, probabilities and deployment costs
PREDICTORS = {}     # model name -> function from one raw command to its intent probabilities


def predict_labels(proba):
    """Predicted intent of each command; ABSTAIN when every intent has the same probability."""
    pred = proba.argmax(axis=1)
    return np.where(np.isclose(proba.max(axis=1), proba.min(axis=1)), ABSTAIN, pred)


def log_loss_on(proba, subset):
    """Average negative log probability of the true intent."""
    return float(-np.mean(np.log(np.clip(proba[subset, y[subset]], 1e-7, 1.0))))


def validation_scores(proba):
    """Training and validation scores of one configuration (never the test set)."""
    pred = predict_labels(proba)
    return {
        "Train accuracy": accuracy_score(y[train_idx], pred[train_idx]),
        "Validation accuracy": accuracy_score(y[val_idx], pred[val_idx]),
        "Validation log loss": log_loss_on(proba, val_idx),
    }


def select_best(table):
    """Highest validation accuracy; ties go to the lower validation log loss."""
    return table.sort_values(["Validation accuracy", "Validation log loss"],
                             ascending=[False, True]).iloc[0]


def selection_reason(table, chosen):
    """One sentence explaining why `chosen` won on the validation set."""
    best = table["Validation accuracy"].max()
    tied = int(np.isclose(table["Validation accuracy"], best).sum())
    close = int((table["Validation accuracy"] >= best - 1 / len(val_idx) - 1e-9).sum())
    reason = f"highest validation accuracy ({best:.3f}) among {len(table)} configurations"
    if tied > 1:
        reason += (f"; {tied} configurations tied, and this one has the lowest validation "
                   f"log loss ({chosen['Validation log loss']:.3f})")
    if close > tied:
        reason += (f"; {close} configurations are within one validation command of the best, "
                   f"so the differences among them are within noise")
    return reason


def register(name, proba, configuration, why, parameters, latency_ms, predictor,
             fit_seconds=None, kind="Model", proba_final=None):
    """
    Record a model's final configuration for the gate (Section 5) and the test (Section 6).

    `proba`: the version fitted on training only -- its validation predictions are honest.
    `proba_final`: the version refit on training + validation -- used for every test score.
    """
    proba_final = proba if proba_final is None else proba_final
    for p in (proba, proba_final):
        assert p.shape == (len(texts), len(CLASSES)), "probabilities must cover every command and every intent"
    FINALISTS[name] = dict(proba=proba, proba_final=proba_final, configuration=configuration, why=why,
                           kind=kind, parameters=parameters, latency_ms=latency_ms, fit_seconds=fit_seconds)
    PREDICTORS[name] = predictor
    scores = validation_scores(proba)
    print(f"Final configuration — {name}")
    print(f"  Chosen:      {configuration}")
    print(f"  Why:         {why}")
    print(f"  Validation:  accuracy {scores['Validation accuracy']:.3f}, "
          f"log loss {scores['Validation log loss']:.3f} "
          f"(training accuracy {scores['Train accuracy']:.3f})")
    print(f"  Deployment:  {parameters:,} parameters, {latency_ms:.2f} ms per command")
    test = test_scores(proba_final)
    print(f"  Test (refit on training + validation): accuracy {test['Test accuracy']:.3f}, unseen commands "
          f"{test['Test accuracy (unseen)']:.3f}, macro F1 {test['Test macro F1']:.3f}")


def test_scores(proba):
    """Test-set scores of a final configuration, before the gate: reported, never used to choose."""
    pred = predict_labels(proba)
    return {
        "Test accuracy": accuracy_score(y[test_idx], pred[test_idx]),
        "Test accuracy (unseen)": accuracy_score(y[test_unseen_idx], pred[test_unseen_idx]),
        "Test macro F1": f1_score(y[test_idx], pred[test_idx], labels=list(range(len(CLASSES))),
                                  average="macro", zero_division=0),
    }


def running_summary():
    """Every final configuration registered so far, scored on the test set (before the gate)."""
    rows = [{"Model": name, "Type": f["kind"],
             "Validation accuracy": validation_scores(f["proba"])["Validation accuracy"],
             **test_scores(f["proba_final"]),
             "Parameters": f["parameters"], "Latency (ms)": f["latency_ms"],
             "Fit time (s)": f["fit_seconds"]}
            for name, f in FINALISTS.items()]
    return (pd.DataFrame(rows).style
            .format({"Validation accuracy": "{:.3f}", "Test accuracy": "{:.3f}",
                     "Test accuracy (unseen)": "{:.3f}", "Test macro F1": "{:.3f}",
                     "Parameters": "{:,.0f}", "Latency (ms)": "{:.2f}", "Fit time (s)": "{:.1f}"},
                    na_rep="—")
            .hide(axis="index")
            .set_caption("Running summary: final configurations so far (validation: fitted on training; test: refit on training + validation), before the confidence gate"))


def measure_latency(predict_one, n=100):
    """Average milliseconds to answer one command, one at a time, as the app would."""
    sample = test_idx[:n]
    predict_one(sample[0])                       # warm-up
    started = time.perf_counter()
    for i in sample:
        predict_one(i)
    return 1000 * (time.perf_counter() - started) / len(sample)

2.1 Two benchmarks¶

The majority benchmark always predicts the most common intent. The classes are perfectly balanced, so it is right only one time in eight.

The keyword rule is the benchmark that matters: the rule a product team could ship on day one without any machine learning. It takes the highest-lift words of each intent from Section 1. A command goes to the intent whose keywords it contains most often. If it contains none, or ties between intents, the rule abstains and the app falls back to help. An abstention is never counted as a prediction of any intent: it is a miss for accuracy, and a fallback for the confidence gate.

The rule has one hyperparameter, the number of keywords per intent, which we choose on the validation set.

In [12]:
majority_class = int(pd.Series(y[train_idx]).mode()[0])
majority_proba = np.zeros((len(dat), len(CLASSES)))
majority_proba[:, majority_class] = 1.0


def keyword_lists(top_n, fit_idx=None):
    """The `top_n` highest-lift words of each intent, learned on `fit_idx` (default: training set)."""
    fit_idx = train_idx if fit_idx is None else fit_idx
    labels = [CLASSES[k] for k in y[fit_idx]]
    return {intent: distinctive_words(texts[fit_idx], labels, intent, top_n=top_n)["word"].tolist()
            for intent in CLASSES}


def keyword_rule(text, keywords):
    """One-hot probabilities if a single intent wins; uniform (= abstain) otherwise."""
    words = set(simple_words(text))
    hits = np.array([len(words & set(keywords[intent])) for intent in CLASSES])
    proba = np.full(len(CLASSES), 1.0 / len(CLASSES))
    if hits.max() > 0 and (hits == hits.max()).sum() == 1:
        proba = np.zeros(len(CLASSES))
        proba[hits.argmax()] = 1.0
    return proba


KEYWORD_GRID = [3, 5, 10, 15, 20]

keyword_rows, keyword_proba = [], {}
for top_n in KEYWORD_GRID:
    keywords = keyword_lists(top_n)
    proba = np.vstack([keyword_rule(t, keywords) for t in texts])
    keyword_proba[top_n] = proba
    keyword_rows.append({
        "Keywords per intent": top_n,
        **validation_scores(proba),
        "Abstains on validation": np.mean(predict_labels(proba[val_idx]) == ABSTAIN),
        "Abstains on unsupported (tuning)": np.mean(predict_labels(proba[unk_tune_idx]) == ABSTAIN),
    })

keyword_results = pd.DataFrame(keyword_rows)
display(keyword_results.style.format({
    "Train accuracy": "{:.3f}", "Validation accuracy": "{:.3f}", "Validation log loss": "{:.2f}",
    "Abstains on validation": "{:.0%}", "Abstains on unsupported (tuning)": "{:.0%}"}).hide(axis="index"))

Interpretation. The keyword rule keeps the most keywords tried (20 per intent, the edge of the grid) and reaches 0.804 on validation but 0.733 on test. It is reliable where one word decides the intent (withdraw, bill, balance: recall 97%) and fails where intents share words: recall is 27% for HELP_SUPPORT, 50% for MANAGE_CONTACTS and 60% for VIEW_TRANSACTIONS. Precision on TRANSFER_MONEY (68%) and WITHDRAW_MONEY (72%) is the costly part: other requests get pulled into money-moving workflows. The majority benchmark is right one time in eight, as expected.

3. Pre-trained Transformers: what we start from¶

Our model does not start from scratch. This section explains what a pre-trained Transformer brings and sets up the fine-tuning recipe.

3.1 Where the knowledge comes from: self-supervised pre-training¶

As in Lecture 12: a Transformer such as BERT was trained on billions of words of English by masking — hiding words and learning to predict them, with the text itself as the answer key. Nobody labelled anything. DistilBERT, the compact version of BERT we fine-tune below, was trained the same way. We can watch it reason about a wallet command.

In [15]:
MLM_MODEL = "distilbert-base-uncased"

mlm_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MLM_MODEL)
mlm_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(MLM_MODEL).to(DEVICE).eval()


def predict_masked_word(sentence, top_n=8):
    """Return the model's most likely fillers for the [MASK] token in `sentence`."""
    encoded = mlm_tokenizer(sentence, return_tensors="pt").to(DEVICE)
    position = (encoded["input_ids"][0] == mlm_tokenizer.mask_token_id).nonzero().item()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = mlm_model(**encoded).logits[0, position]
    probabilities = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    top = torch.topk(probabilities, top_n)
    return [mlm_tokenizer.decode([i]) for i in top.indices], top.values.float().cpu().numpy()


for sentence in ["I want to [MASK] 50 dollars to my sister .",
                 "Please [MASK] my electricity bill .",
                 "My transfer [MASK] , who do I call for help ?"]:
    words, probabilities = predict_masked_word(sentence)
    print(sentence)
    print("   " + ", ".join(f"{w} ({p:.0%})" for w, p in zip(words, probabilities)))
    print()

del mlm_model

DistilBERT has never seen a Sole command, yet it already knows that one sends money to a sister, pays a bill, and that a transfer that needs help has failed. That knowledge came for free.

3.2 The pipeline: from a command to a prediction¶

Stage What happens Who owns it
Tokenizer text becomes model-specific token IDs, with special tokens, padding and truncation shipped with the model
Encoder stacked Transformer blocks turn IDs into one contextual vector per token pre-trained
Pooling the per-token vectors are collapsed into one vector per command our choice
Classification head a small network maps that vector to eight intent probabilities trained by us

DistilBERT's WordPiece tokenizer (the same as BERT's) splits rare words into known pieces, so a name like Savenaca never becomes [UNK].

In [16]:

}

    "Token ID": encoded_example["input_ids"][0].numpy(),

}).T)

DistilBERT is a compressed copy of BERT: half the blocks, trained to imitate BERT's outputs. Lecture 12 found that it keeps most of BERT's accuracy at a fraction of the cost, which is why it is the pre-trained model we fine-tune.

3.3 The fine-tuning recipe¶

Fine-tuning lets our labelled commands update the pre-trained weights themselves, not just a head on top.

Pre-training Fine-tuning
Data billions of words, unlabelled 1,920 commands, labelled
Objective predict masked words predict the user's intent
Supplies knowledge of English knowledge of our task
Cost days on a large GPU cluster minutes on one GPU

A fresh eight-intent classifier is placed on the [CLS] vector. Three hyperparameters are chosen on validation:

Hyperparameter Values What it controls
how much to unfreeze frozen backbone (classifier only); top 2 blocks; full model how far the pre-trained knowledge may move
learning rate frozen: 0.0003, 0.001, 0.003; top 2 and full: 0.00002–0.0001 (three values each) step size of AdamW, with 10% linear warm-up then linear decay
epochs up to 10 (frozen) or 6 (unfrozen) the validation set is scored after every epoch, and the best epoch is kept

Pre-trained weights must be moved gently, hence the small learning rates; a fresh classifier on a frozen backbone trains at the usual rate and needs more epochs. That is 9 configurations, each trained once, with the best epoch kept. The winner is then refit on training + validation with the same strategy and learning rate, stopping at the chosen epoch.

In [17]:
from transformers import get_linear_schedule_with_warmup

FINE_TUNE_BATCH = 16

STRATEGY_GRID = {
    "Frozen backbone": dict(unfrozen_blocks=0,    learning_rates=[3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3], epochs=10),
    "Top 2 blocks":    dict(unfrozen_blocks=2,    learning_rates=[2e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4], epochs=6),
    "Full model":      dict(unfrozen_blocks=None, learning_rates=[2e-5, 3e-5, 5e-5], epochs=6),
}


def encoder_blocks(model, model_name):
    """The list of Transformer blocks inside a sequence-classification model."""
    base = model.base_model
    return base.transformer.layer if "distilbert" in model_name else base.encoder.layer


def build_classifier(model_name, unfrozen_blocks):
    """
    Load a pre-trained encoder with a fresh eight-intent head on top, and decide
    which parts of it the optimizer is allowed to move.

    `unfrozen_blocks = 0` freezes the whole encoder; `None` unfreezes everything.
    """
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)
    model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        num_labels=len(CLASSES),
        id2label=dict(enumerate(CLASSES)),
        label2id={c: i for i, c in enumerate(CLASSES)},
        attn_implementation="eager"
    )
    if unfrozen_blocks is not None:
        for parameter in model.base_model.embeddings.parameters():
            parameter.requires_grad = False
        blocks = encoder_blocks(model, model_name)
        for block in blocks[:len(blocks) - unfrozen_blocks]:
            for parameter in block.parameters():
                parameter.requires_grad = False
    return model.to(DEVICE)


def tokenize_corpus(model_name):
    """Token IDs and attention masks for every command, for one model."""
    local_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    encoded = local_tokenizer(list(texts), padding="max_length", truncation=True,
                              max_length=MAX_TOKENS_BERT, return_tensors="pt")
    return local_tokenizer, encoded["input_ids"], encoded["attention_mask"]


@torch.no_grad()
def predict_proba_torch(model, input_ids, attention_mask, subset, batch_size=128):
    """Intent probabilities for a subset of the commands."""
    model.eval()
    output = []
    for start in range(0, len(subset), batch_size):
        rows = subset[start:start + batch_size]
        logits = model(input_ids=input_ids[rows].to(DEVICE),
                       attention_mask=attention_mask[rows].to(DEVICE)).logits
        output.append(torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1).float().cpu().numpy())
    return np.vstack(output)


@torch.no_grad()
def torch_predict_one(model, local_tokenizer, text):
    """One command end to end, as the app would: tokenize, encode, classify."""
    encoded = local_tokenizer([text], truncation=True, max_length=MAX_TOKENS_BERT, return_tensors="pt")
    logits = model(input_ids=encoded["input_ids"].to(DEVICE),
                   attention_mask=encoded["attention_mask"].to(DEVICE)).logits
    return torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1).float().cpu().numpy()


def fine_tune(model_name, unfrozen_blocks, learning_rate, epochs, input_ids, attention_mask):
    """
    Fine-tune on the training commands. After every epoch the validation set is scored,
    and the epoch with the best validation accuracy (ties: lower log loss) is kept.
    """
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)
    np.random.seed(SEED)
    model = build_classifier(model_name, unfrozen_blocks)
    loader = DataLoader(
        TensorDataset(input_ids[train_idx], attention_mask[train_idx], torch.tensor(y[train_idx])),
        batch_size=FINE_TUNE_BATCH, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED)
    )
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad], lr=learning_rate)
    total_steps = epochs * len(loader)
    scheduler = get_linear_schedule_with_warmup(optimizer, int(0.1 * total_steps), total_steps)
    trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)

    history, best = [], None
    started = time.time()
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        for batch_ids, batch_mask, batch_labels in loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = model(input_ids=batch_ids.to(DEVICE), attention_mask=batch_mask.to(DEVICE),
                         labels=batch_labels.to(DEVICE)).loss
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            scheduler.step()

        val_proba = predict_proba_torch(model, input_ids, attention_mask, val_idx)
        accuracy = accuracy_score(y[val_idx], val_proba.argmax(axis=1))
        log_loss = float(-np.mean(np.log(np.clip(val_proba[np.arange(len(val_idx)), y[val_idx]], 1e-7, 1))))
        history.append({"Epoch": epoch, "Validation accuracy": accuracy, "Validation log loss": log_loss})
        if best is None or (accuracy, -log_loss) > (best["accuracy"], -best["log_loss"]):
            best = {"accuracy": accuracy, "log_loss": log_loss, "epoch": epoch,
                    "proba": predict_proba_torch(model, input_ids, attention_mask, np.arange(len(texts))),
                    "state": {k: v.detach().to("cpu", copy=True) for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}}

    return model, best, history, trainable, time.time() - started


def run_finetuning_grid(label):
    """Every strategy x learning rate for one pre-trained model; the winner is kept in memory."""
    model_name = PRETRAINED_MODELS[label]
    local_tokenizer, input_ids, attention_mask = tokenize_corpus(model_name)
    rows, histories, probas = [], [], {}
    best_so_far, winner = None, None

    for strategy, settings in STRATEGY_GRID.items():
        for learning_rate in settings["learning_rates"]:
            key = f"{strategy} | lr={learning_rate:g}"
            print(f"Fine-tuning {label} — {key} ...", flush=True)
            model, best, history, trainable, elapsed = fine_tune(
                model_name, settings["unfrozen_blocks"], learning_rate, settings["epochs"],
                input_ids, attention_mask
            )
            probas[key] = best["proba"]
            histories += [{"Strategy": strategy, "Learning rate": learning_rate, **h} for h in history]
            row = {
                "Strategy": strategy, "Learning rate": learning_rate,
                "Epochs tried": settings["epochs"], "Best epoch": best["epoch"],
                "Parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()),
                "Trainable parameters": trainable, "Training time (s)": elapsed,
                **validation_scores(best["proba"]),
            }
            rows.append(row)

            # Keep the best epoch of the best configuration so far (weights on the CPU)
            score = (row["Validation accuracy"], -row["Validation log loss"])
            if best_so_far is None or score > best_so_far:
                best_so_far = score
                winner = {"unfrozen_blocks": settings["unfrozen_blocks"], "state": best["state"]}
            del model, best
            if DEVICE.type == "mps":
                torch.mps.empty_cache()

    # Rebuild the winning model from its weights
    final_model = build_classifier(model_name, winner["unfrozen_blocks"])
    final_model.load_state_dict(winner["state"])
    final_model.eval()
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), pd.DataFrame(histories), probas, final_model, local_tokenizer, input_ids, attention_mask


def show_finetuning(results):
    return (results.sort_values(["Validation accuracy", "Validation log loss"], ascending=[False, True])
            .style.format({"Learning rate": "{:g}", "Parameters": "{:,}", "Trainable parameters": "{:,}",
                           "Training time (s)": "{:.0f}", "Train accuracy": "{:.3f}",
                           "Validation accuracy": "{:.3f}", "Validation log loss": "{:.3f}"})
            .hide(axis="index"))


def plot_finetuning(history, chosen, label):
    """Validation accuracy after every epoch, for every strategy and learning rate."""
    strategy_colors = dict(zip(STRATEGY_GRID, [INK_SECONDARY, ACCENT_LIGHT, ACCENT]))
    styles = ["-", "--", ":"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6.5))
    for strategy, settings in STRATEGY_GRID.items():
        for k, learning_rate in enumerate(settings["learning_rates"]):
            run = history[(history["Strategy"] == strategy) & np.isclose(history["Learning rate"], learning_rate)]
            ax.plot(run["Epoch"], run["Validation accuracy"], color=strategy_colors[strategy],
                    linestyle=styles[k % 3], linewidth=2.2, marker="o", markersize=4,
                    label=f"{strategy}, lr {learning_rate:g}")
    ax.scatter([chosen["Best epoch"]], [chosen["Validation accuracy"]], s=220, facecolor="none",
               edgecolor=INK, linewidth=2.5, zorder=5, label="Chosen")
    ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
    ax.set_ylabel("Validation accuracy")
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=FONTSIZE)
    ax.legend(fontsize=FONTSIZE - 4, loc="lower right", ncol=2)
    ax.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    save_figure(fig, f"0{8 if label == 'DistilBERT' else 9}_{label.lower()}_finetuning")
    plt.show()


def refit_finetuned(model_name, strategy, learning_rate, stop_epoch, input_ids, attention_mask):
    """
    Refit the chosen configuration on training + validation. The learning-rate schedule spans the
    same number of epochs as in the grid, and training stops at the epoch chosen on validation,
    so the refit follows the same path as the winning run.
    """
    settings = STRATEGY_GRID[strategy]
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)
    np.random.seed(SEED)
    model = build_classifier(model_name, settings["unfrozen_blocks"])
    loader = DataLoader(
        TensorDataset(input_ids[REFIT_IDX], attention_mask[REFIT_IDX], torch.tensor(y[REFIT_IDX])),
        batch_size=FINE_TUNE_BATCH, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED)
    )
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad], lr=learning_rate)
    total_steps = settings["epochs"] * len(loader)
    scheduler = get_linear_schedule_with_warmup(optimizer, int(0.1 * total_steps), total_steps)

    started = time.time()
    model.train()
    for _ in range(stop_epoch):
        for batch_ids, batch_mask, batch_labels in loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = model(input_ids=batch_ids.to(DEVICE), attention_mask=batch_mask.to(DEVICE),
                         labels=batch_labels.to(DEVICE)).loss
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            scheduler.step()
    model.eval()
    return model, time.time() - started


FINETUNED = {}      # model name -> (refit model, tokenizer)


def register_finetuned(label, results, probas, model, local_tokenizer, input_ids, attention_mask):
    """Check the winning model in memory, time it, and register its final configuration."""
    chosen = select_best(results)
    key = f"{chosen['Strategy']} | lr={chosen['Learning rate']:g}"
    restored = predict_proba_torch(model, input_ids, attention_mask, val_idx)
    assert np.allclose(restored, probas[key][val_idx], atol=1e-3), "restored model does not match the grid"

    # Refit on training + validation; the training-only model is no longer needed
    del model
    if DEVICE.type == "mps":
        torch.mps.empty_cache()
    print(f"Refitting {label} on training + validation for {int(chosen['Best epoch'])} epochs ...")
    model, refit_seconds = refit_finetuned(PRETRAINED_MODELS[label], chosen["Strategy"], chosen["Learning rate"],
                                           int(chosen["Best epoch"]), input_ids, attention_mask)
    proba_final = predict_proba_torch(model, input_ids, attention_mask, np.arange(len(texts)))

    name = f"Fine-tuned {label}"
    FINETUNED[name] = (model, local_tokenizer)     # kept so the deployed model can be saved
    register(name, probas[key],
             configuration=(f"{chosen['Strategy'].lower()}, learning rate {chosen['Learning rate']:g}, "
                            f"{chosen['Best epoch']} epochs ({chosen['Trainable parameters']:,} of "
                            f"{chosen['Parameters']:,} parameters trained)"),
             why=selection_reason(results, chosen),
             parameters=int(chosen["Parameters"]),
             latency_ms=measure_latency(lambda i: torch_predict_one(model, local_tokenizer, texts[i]), n=50),
             predictor=lambda text: torch_predict_one(model, local_tokenizer, text)[0],
             fit_seconds=refit_seconds, proba_final=proba_final)
    return name

4. Fine-tuned DistilBERT¶

How it is built. DistilBERT's WordPiece tokenizer turns the command into sub-word tokens (so Savenaca becomes known pieces, never [UNK]); six pre-trained Transformer blocks produce a contextual vector per token; the [CLS] vector feeds a fresh classifier (a 768-unit layer, then the eight-intent softmax). The recipe and the grid are those of Section 3.3: 3 strategies × 3 learning rates, best epoch kept.

This is the slowest part of the notebook. The winning model is kept in memory for the gate and the demo.

Interpretation. Unfreezing the full model at learning rate 5e-05 wins on validation (0.925, log loss 0.223), with the best epoch at 2 of 6. Top 2 blocks comes close (0.912, about three commands behind), and the frozen backbone trails (0.896): letting the pre-trained weights move pays off. Training accuracy is 1.000, so the model fits the training commands perfectly.

Refit on training + validation, it scores 0.992 on test (macro F1 0.992): 2 errors in 240 commands, against 0.733 for the keyword rule. The jump from validation (0.925) to test is larger than noise alone would explain. The refit sees 12.5% more data, and the test commands seem easier than the validation ones. The validation figure is the conservative estimate. The model is large (67 million parameters), but answers a command in 5.6 ms on Colab's GPU.

5. The confidence gate: knowing when not to act¶

Accuracy answers "when the request is one we support, how often is the intent right?". In the app, two more questions matter as much:

  • When the model is unsure, can it say so, and send the user to clarification or help instead of guessing?
  • When the user asks for something we do not support, does the model refuse, or does it confidently open a workflow?

Every model outputs a probability for each intent, and the largest is a usable confidence. The deck's system flow puts a confidence gate after the classifier: above a threshold the app opens the predicted workflow; below it, the app falls back to clarification / help.

Everything in this section uses the validation pool only: the validation commands plus the unsupported commands set aside for tuning. First, the problem the dataset README warns about — overconfidence on unsupported commands.

5.1 Calibrating the confidences¶

A confidence of 0.98 should mean "right 98% of the time". Neural networks trained to minimize log loss on a small training set are typically overconfident: their largest probability sits near 1 even when they are wrong, and the confidences of different models are not on the same scale. A threshold chosen on such numbers ends up squeezed into the last few thousandths below 1.

Temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017) fixes this with a single parameter per model. The log-probabilities are divided by a temperature $T$ before the softmax:

$$p_k^{\text{calibrated}} \propto \exp\left(\frac{\log p_k}{T}\right)$$

$T > 1$ softens overconfident probabilities, and $T < 1$ sharpens underconfident ones. $T$ is fitted on the supported validation commands to minimize log loss; the unsupported commands are not used, because they have no correct intent. Temperature scaling never changes which intent is predicted — only how confident the model says it is — so accuracy is unchanged. The benchmarks output only 0s and 1s (or a uniform abstention) and are left as they are.

We report the log loss and the expected calibration error (ECE: the average gap between confidence and accuracy, over ten confidence bins) before and after. Both are measured on the same validation commands used to fit $T$, so they show the fit, not an out-of-sample guarantee; Section 6 checks the result on test. The temperature is fitted on the training-only model, whose validation predictions are honest, and applied unchanged to the model refit on training + validation.

In [23]:
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar


def apply_temperature(proba, temperature):
    """Rescale probabilities by a temperature; the predicted intent does not change."""
    logits = np.log(np.clip(proba, 1e-12, 1.0)) / temperature
    logits -= logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    exponentiated = np.exp(logits)
    return exponentiated / exponentiated.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)


def fit_temperature(proba):
    """The temperature that minimizes log loss on the supported validation commands."""
    result = minimize_scalar(lambda log_t: log_loss_on(apply_temperature(proba, np.exp(log_t)), val_idx),
                             bounds=(-4, 4), method="bounded")
    return float(np.exp(result.x))


def expected_calibration_error(proba, subset, bins=10):
    """Average |accuracy - confidence| over confidence bins, weighted by bin size."""
    confidence = proba[subset].max(axis=1)
    correct = proba[subset].argmax(axis=1) == y[subset]
    edges = np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)
    error = 0.0
    for low, high in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        in_bin = (confidence > low) & (confidence <= high)
        if in_bin.any():
            error += in_bin.mean() * abs(correct[in_bin].mean() - confidence[in_bin].mean())
    return error


TEMPERATURE, GATE_PROBA, GATE_PROBA_FINAL = {}, {}, {}
calibration_rows = []
for name, finalist in FINALISTS.items():
    raw = finalist["proba"]
    if finalist["kind"] == "Benchmark":
        TEMPERATURE[name], GATE_PROBA[name], GATE_PROBA_FINAL[name] = 1.0, raw, finalist["proba_final"]
        continue
    temperature = fit_temperature(raw)
    calibrated = apply_temperature(raw, temperature)
    TEMPERATURE[name], GATE_PROBA[name] = temperature, calibrated
    # The temperature fitted on the training-only model is applied to the refit model used on test
    GATE_PROBA_FINAL[name] = apply_temperature(finalist["proba_final"], temperature)
    calibration_rows.append({
        "Model": name, "Temperature": temperature,
        "Val log loss (raw)": log_loss_on(raw, val_idx),
        "Val log loss (calibrated)": log_loss_on(calibrated, val_idx),
        "Val ECE (raw)": expected_calibration_error(raw, val_idx),

    })

5.2 Putting a price on each outcome¶

Every command ends in one of five outcomes. We price each relative to today's status quo, where the user navigates the menus by hand. These are illustrative assumptions for Sole to replace with its own numbers; the method does not depend on them.

Outcome Value per command
Supported command, routed to the right workflow + VALUE_CORRECT (navigation time saved, higher completion)
Supported command, sent to fallback − COST_FALLBACK (one extra step for the user)
Supported command, routed to the wrong read-only workflow − COST_WRONG_INFO
Any command routed to the wrong money-moving workflow − COST_WRONG_MONEY (confusion, support contact, lost trust)
Unsupported command, rejected 0 (the right answer)
Unsupported command, routed to a workflow − COST_WRONG_INFO or − COST_WRONG_MONEY

The threshold is a hyperparameter like any other: it is chosen on the validation pool (validation commands plus the unsupported commands set aside for tuning) and applied unchanged to the test pool in Section 6. When the keyword rule abstains, the app always falls back.

In [24]:
COMMANDS_PER_DAY = 5_000          # Smart Actions commands typed per day -- Sole's number
DAYS_PER_YEAR = 365
SHARE_UNSUPPORTED = 0.10          # share of commands the app cannot serve -- measure in a pilot

VALUE_CORRECT = 0.10              # $ per command routed straight to the right workflow
COST_FALLBACK = 0.05              # $ per supported command sent to clarification / help
COST_WRONG_INFO = 0.50            # $ per command opening the wrong read-only workflow
COST_WRONG_MONEY = 5.00           # $ per command opening the wrong money-moving workflow

MONEY_MOVING_IDS = [CLASSES.index(c) for c in MONEY_MOVING]
THRESHOLDS = np.round(np.concatenate([np.arange(0.0, 0.95, 0.005), np.arange(0.95, 1.0, 0.001)]), 4)


def gate_outcomes(proba, subset, threshold):
    """Share of each outcome when the gate opens a workflow only above `threshold`."""
    p, truth = proba[subset], y[subset]
    confidence, pred = p.max(axis=1), predict_labels(p)
    accept = (confidence >= threshold) & (pred != ABSTAIN)
    supported, unsupported = truth >= 0, truth < 0
    money = np.isin(pred, MONEY_MOVING_IDS)
    wrong = supported & accept & (pred != truth)
    return {
        "Routed correctly": (supported & accept & (pred == truth)).sum() / supported.sum(),
        "Fallback": (supported & ~accept).sum() / supported.sum(),
        "Wrong workflow": wrong.sum() / supported.sum(),
        "Wrong money workflow": (wrong & money).sum() / supported.sum(),
        "Unsupported rejected": (unsupported & ~accept).sum() / unsupported.sum(),
        "Unsupported accepted": (unsupported & accept).sum() / unsupported.sum(),
        "Unsupported into money workflow": (unsupported & accept & money).sum() / unsupported.sum(),
    }


def value_per_command(o, cost_wrong_money=None):
    """Expected dollar value of one command, given the shares of each outcome."""
    cost_money = COST_WRONG_MONEY if cost_wrong_money is None else cost_wrong_money
    supported = (o["Routed correctly"] * VALUE_CORRECT
                 - o["Fallback"] * COST_FALLBACK
                 - (o["Wrong workflow"] - o["Wrong money workflow"]) * COST_WRONG_INFO
                 - o["Wrong money workflow"] * cost_money)
    unsupported = -((o["Unsupported accepted"] - o["Unsupported into money workflow"]) * COST_WRONG_INFO
                    + o["Unsupported into money workflow"] * cost_money)
    return (1 - SHARE_UNSUPPORTED) * supported + SHARE_UNSUPPORTED * unsupported


def choose_threshold(proba, cost_wrong_money=None):
    """The confidence cutoff with the highest value on the validation pool."""
    values = [value_per_command(gate_outcomes(proba, gate_val_idx, t), cost_wrong_money)
              for t in THRESHOLDS]
    return float(THRESHOLDS[int(np.argmax(values))]), float(np.max(values))

5.3 A threshold for every model¶

For each final model we choose the threshold that maximizes value on the validation pool, with calibrated confidences. For comparison, the first columns show what the same rule picks on the raw confidences.

5.4 Which model to deploy¶

The deployment decision is made on validation, before looking at the test set: the model with the highest validation value. When several are within 2% of the best, the tie goes to the fastest — the same logic Lecture 12 used to prefer DistilBERT over BERT.

In [26]:
def deployment_choice(table, value_column="Validation value / 1,000"):
    """Highest validation value; within 2% of the best, the fastest wins."""
    best = table[value_column].max()
    contenders = table[table[value_column] >= best - 0.02 * abs(best)]
    return contenders.sort_values("Latency (ms)").iloc[0], contenders


DEPLOYED, contenders = deployment_choice(gate_results)

DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD = float(DEPLOYED["Threshold"])

          f"{row['Latency (ms)']:.1f} ms")
print(f"\nDeployed: {DEPLOYED_NAME}, calibrated confidence threshold {DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD:.3f} "
      f"(temperature {TEMPERATURE[DEPLOYED_NAME]:.2f})")

6. Final comparison on the test set¶

The running summaries scored each classifier on its own. This section adds the confidence gate on the test pool and compares the final models side by side. Each model enters with its final configuration (Sections 2–4), refit on training + validation, and its threshold (Section 5), both fixed on validation. The test pool is the test commands plus the held-out unsupported commands. Section 6.9 then adds a middle tier to the deployed model's gate: a short menu.

Fine-tuned DistilBERT full model, learning rate 5e-05, 2 epochs (66,959,624 of 66,959,624 parameters trained) highest validation accuracy (0.925) among 9 configurations

6.2 Classification quality, safety and cost¶

The first three columns are the classifier alone (before the gate). The next block is what users experience after the gate, as a share of the supported test commands: routed correctly, routed to a wrong workflow, sent to fallback, and — the subset of wrong routes that matters most — opened a money-moving workflow by mistake. The last block is the held-out unsupported commands, then the dollar value.

6.3 Where each model goes wrong: confusion matrices after the gate¶

One matrix per model, on the test pool. Rows are what the user wanted (the eight intents, plus unsupported requests); columns are what the app did (an intent, or fallback). Each cell is the percentage of its row: the diagonal is the share routed correctly, the last column the share sent to fallback, and every other cell a wrong route. Money-moving intents are marked with $. For unsupported requests, the fallback column is the right answer.

In [29]:
def app_actions(proba, subset, threshold):
    """The action the app takes: an intent index, or len(CLASSES) for fallback."""
    p = proba[subset]
    pred = predict_labels(p)
    return np.where((p.max(axis=1) >= threshold) & (pred != ABSTAIN), pred, len(CLASSES))


row_labels = [f"{c} $" if c in MONEY_MOVING else c for c in CLASSES] + ["UNSUPPORTED"]
col_labels = [f"{c} $" if c in MONEY_MOVING else c for c in CLASSES] + ["FALLBACK"]
truth_test = np.where(y[gate_test_idx] >= 0, y[gate_test_idx], len(CLASSES))
matrix_models = [n for n in FINALISTS if n != MAJORITY_NAME]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(matrix_models), figsize=(12 * len(matrix_models), 12), squeeze=False)
for ax, name in zip(axes.ravel(), matrix_models):
    threshold = float(gate_results.set_index("Model").loc[name, "Threshold"])
    actions = app_actions(GATE_PROBA_FINAL[name], gate_test_idx, threshold)
    counts = confusion_matrix(truth_test, actions, labels=range(len(CLASSES) + 1))
    share = 100 * counts / counts.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sns.heatmap(share, annot=np.where(counts > 0, np.char.mod("%.0f", share), ""), fmt="",
                cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=100, square=True, linewidths=1, linecolor="white",
                xticklabels=col_labels, yticklabels=row_labels, cbar=False,

    o = final_results.set_index("Model").loc[name]

6.5 Recall and precision by intent¶

The classifier alone, before the gate. Recall (sensitivity): of the commands that wanted this intent, the share predicted as this intent. Precision: of the commands predicted as this intent, the share that wanted it. Low precision on a money-moving intent means other requests are being pulled into a money flow; that is what the gate must catch. The keyword rule's abstentions count as misses for recall.

Interpretation. The decision does not depend on the cost of a money-moving error. From $0.50 to $50, the deployed model is DistilBERT, with the same threshold (0.940) and the same test results. Above that threshold DistilBERT routes no validation command into a wrong workflow, so a higher penalty has nothing to act on. The keyword rule never changes either (threshold 0): its outputs are 0 or 1, so there is no confidence to cut on.

6.8 Conclusion: which model to deploy¶

Deploy fine-tuned DistilBERT. It is the only option that creates value. With the two-way gate it routes 94.2% of supported test commands correctly, sends 5.8% to fallback, and opens no wrong workflow for a supported command. That is worth about $139k a year at 5,000 commands a day. Both benchmarks lose money. The keyword rule sends 8.8% of supported commands into the wrong money workflow, at −$807k a year. Always predicting TRANSFER_MONEY loses −$8.1M. The choice holds for any cost of a money-moving error between $0.50 and $50 (6.7). Its price is size (67 million parameters), not speed (5.6 ms per command). Its weak spot is unsupported requests: 12% still open a workflow, almost always HELP_SUPPORT, and never a money flow.

6.9 A three-tier gate: open, menu, or "not understood"¶

The gate above has two outcomes, so a command the model is almost sure about gets the same help screen as nonsense. A middle tier fixes that. For the deployed model:

  • Confidence ≥ open threshold → open the predicted workflow (as before).
  • Menu threshold ≤ confidence < open threshold → show a short menu with the MENU_SIZE most likely intents plus "something else". The user chooses, so the menu never opens a wrong workflow by itself.
  • Confidence < menu threshold → "we did not understand": ask to rephrase, or offer help.

The menu has its own prices (again illustrative assumptions for Sole to replace): a menu that contains the right intent is worth a bit less than a direct route (one extra tap); a menu without it costs a bit more than a plain fallback (a wasted screen); an unsupported command shown the menu costs a little. Both thresholds are chosen together on the validation pool and applied unchanged to test. Setting both thresholds equal recovers the two-way gate, so the three-tier gate can only match or beat it on validation.

In [35]:
MENU_SIZE = 3                     # intents offered in the menu, plus "something else"
VALUE_MENU_HIT = 0.07             # $ per supported command whose intent is in the menu (one extra tap)
COST_MENU_MISS = 0.07             # $ per supported command whose intent is not in the menu (menu, then help)
COST_MENU_UNSUPPORTED = 0.02      # $ per unsupported command shown the menu before help
MENU_GRID = np.union1d(np.round(np.arange(0.0, 1.0, 0.01), 2), THRESHOLDS)   # includes every open threshold, so the two-way gate is always a candidate


def tiered_outcomes(proba, subset, open_threshold, menu_threshold):
    """Share of each outcome with three tiers: open the workflow, show a menu, or 'not understood'."""
    p, truth = proba[subset], y[subset]
    confidence, pred = p.max(axis=1), predict_labels(p)
    decided = pred != ABSTAIN
    open_ = decided & (confidence >= open_threshold)
    menu = decided & ~open_ & (confidence >= menu_threshold)
    in_menu = (np.argsort(-p, axis=1)[:, :MENU_SIZE] == truth[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    supported, unsupported = truth >= 0, truth < 0
    money = np.isin(pred, MONEY_MOVING_IDS)
    wrong = supported & open_ & (pred != truth)
    n_supported, n_unsupported = supported.sum(), unsupported.sum()
    return {
        "Open, correct": (supported & open_ & (pred == truth)).sum() / n_supported,
        "Menu, intent offered": (supported & menu & in_menu).sum() / n_supported,
        "Menu, intent missing": (supported & menu & ~in_menu).sum() / n_supported,
        "Not understood": (supported & ~open_ & ~menu).sum() / n_supported,
        "Wrong workflow": wrong.sum() / n_supported,
        "Wrong money workflow": (wrong & money).sum() / n_supported,
        "Unsupported: not understood": (unsupported & ~open_ & ~menu).sum() / n_unsupported,
        "Unsupported: menu": (unsupported & menu).sum() / n_unsupported,
        "Unsupported accepted": (unsupported & open_).sum() / n_unsupported,
        "Unsupported into money workflow": (unsupported & open_ & money).sum() / n_unsupported,
    }


def tiered_value(o):
    """Expected dollar value of one command under the three-tier gate."""
    supported = (o["Open, correct"] * VALUE_CORRECT
                 + o["Menu, intent offered"] * VALUE_MENU_HIT
                 - o["Menu, intent missing"] * COST_MENU_MISS
                 - o["Not understood"] * COST_FALLBACK
                 - (o["Wrong workflow"] - o["Wrong money workflow"]) * COST_WRONG_INFO
                 - o["Wrong money workflow"] * COST_WRONG_MONEY)
    unsupported = -(o["Unsupported: menu"] * COST_MENU_UNSUPPORTED
                    + (o["Unsupported accepted"] - o["Unsupported into money workflow"]) * COST_WRONG_INFO
                    + o["Unsupported into money workflow"] * COST_WRONG_MONEY)
    return (1 - SHARE_UNSUPPORTED) * supported + SHARE_UNSUPPORTED * unsupported


def choose_tiers(proba):
    """Open and menu thresholds with the highest value on the validation pool.
    Ties go to the lowest open threshold (as in Section 5), then to the highest menu threshold."""
    best_value, best_open, best_menu = -np.inf, None, None
    for t_open in THRESHOLDS:
        for t_menu in MENU_GRID[MENU_GRID <= t_open][::-1]:
            value = tiered_value(tiered_outcomes(proba, gate_val_idx, t_open, t_menu))
            if value > best_value + 1e-12:
                best_value, best_open, best_menu = value, float(t_open), float(t_menu)
    return best_open, best_menu, best_value


# Sanity check: with both thresholds equal, the three-tier gate is the two-way gate of Section 5
_o = tiered_outcomes(GATE_PROBA[DEPLOYED_NAME], gate_val_idx, DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD, DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD)
assert np.isclose(tiered_value(_o), value_per_command(
    gate_outcomes(GATE_PROBA[DEPLOYED_NAME], gate_val_idx, DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD)))

OPEN_THRESHOLD, MENU_THRESHOLD, _ = choose_tiers(GATE_PROBA[DEPLOYED_NAME])

tier_rows = []
for gate, (t_open, t_menu) in [("Two-way gate (Section 5)", (DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD, DEPLOYED_THRESHOLD)),
                               ("Three-tier gate", (OPEN_THRESHOLD, MENU_THRESHOLD))]:
    for pool, proba, subset in [("Validation", GATE_PROBA[DEPLOYED_NAME], gate_val_idx),
                                ("Test", GATE_PROBA_FINAL[DEPLOYED_NAME], gate_test_idx)]:
        o = tiered_outcomes(proba, subset, t_open, t_menu)
        value = tiered_value(o)
        tier_rows.append({"Gate": gate, "Pool": pool, "Open threshold": t_open, "Menu threshold": t_menu, **o,
                          "Value / 1,000": 1000 * value,
                          "Annual value": value * COMMANDS_PER_DAY * DAYS_PER_YEAR})
tier_results = pd.DataFrame(tier_rows)
tier_share_columns = [c for c in tier_results.columns if c not in
                      ("Gate", "Pool", "Open threshold", "Menu threshold", "Value / 1,000", "Annual value")]
display(tier_results.style.format({
    "Open threshold": "{:.3f}", "Menu threshold": "{:.2f}",
    **{c: "{:.1%}" for c in tier_share_columns},
    "Value / 1,000": "${:,.1f}", "Annual value": "${:,.0f}"}).hide(axis="index")
    .set_caption(f"{DEPLOYED_NAME}: two-way vs three-tier gate (thresholds chosen on validation)"))

print(f"Three-tier gate for {DEPLOYED_NAME} (calibrated confidence):")
print(f"  >= {OPEN_THRESHOLD:.3f}            open the predicted workflow")
print(f"  {MENU_THRESHOLD:.2f} to {OPEN_THRESHOLD:.3f}     menu with the top {MENU_SIZE} intents + 'something else'")
print(f"  <  {MENU_THRESHOLD:.2f}             'not understood': rephrase / help")

Interpretation. Adding the menu moves the open threshold up, from 0.940 to 0.963, and the menu covers 0.45 to 0.963. On test:

  • Supported commands: 93.3% open directly and 6.7% get the menu, which always contains the right intent. None end in "not understood", and none open a wrong workflow. The 5.8% that fell back under the two-way gate now reach their workflow in one extra tap.
  • Unsupported commands: those that open a workflow fall from 12.0% to 6.7% (none into a money flow). 69% now see the menu and 24% get "not understood".
  • Value: $83.5 per 1,000 commands against $76.1, or about $152k a year against $139k.

The gain rests on the menu prices we assumed. In particular, showing the menu to an out-of-scope request costs only $0.02, which is why almost every low-confidence command gets the menu. If Sole finds that menu more annoying, the menu threshold will rise and "not understood" will take a larger share.

7. Try it: the routing function behind the demo¶

The deck's system flow, end to end, with the deployed model: a command goes in, the model predicts an intent, its confidence is calibrated with the model's temperature, and the three-tier gate (Section 6.9) decides whether to open the workflow, show a short menu, or say it did not understand.

In [37]:
NOT_UNDERSTOOD = "not understood: ask to rephrase / help"


def route(command, name=None):
    """Intent, calibrated confidence and the action the app would take for one command."""
    name = name or DEPLOYED_NAME
    if name == DEPLOYED_NAME:
        open_threshold, menu_threshold = OPEN_THRESHOLD, MENU_THRESHOLD
    else:   # other models keep their two-way gate from Section 5
        open_threshold = menu_threshold = float(gate_results.set_index("Model").loc[name, "Threshold"])
    proba = apply_temperature(PREDICTORS[name](command)[None, :], TEMPERATURE[name])
    pred, confidence = int(predict_labels(proba)[0]), float(proba.max())
    if pred == ABSTAIN:
        return "—", confidence, NOT_UNDERSTOOD
    intent = CLASSES[pred]
    if confidence >= open_threshold:
        action = f"open {intent}"
    elif confidence >= menu_threshold:
        options = [CLASSES[k] for k in np.argsort(-proba[0])[:MENU_SIZE]]
        action = "menu: " + " / ".join(options) + " / something else"
    else:
        action = NOT_UNDERSTOOD
    return intent, confidence, action


print(f"Routing with {DEPLOYED_NAME} (open >= {OPEN_THRESHOLD:.3f}, menu >= {MENU_THRESHOLD:.2f})\n")
for command in ["Send 20 to my mum", "transfer didn't go through", "how much do I have",
                "show what I withdrew last week", "pay fiji water", "who paid into the church group",
                "book me a taxi", "what's the weather tomorrow"]:
    intent, confidence, action = route(command)
    print(f"{command:35s} -> {intent:18s} {confidence:6.1%}   {action}")

# Save what the demo needs: the deployed model (half precision, about 135 MB) and its routing settings
import copy
import json

DEPLOY_DIR = os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "models", "deployed")
os.makedirs(DEPLOY_DIR, exist_ok=True)
routing = {
    "model": DEPLOYED_NAME, "classes": CLASSES, "money_moving": MONEY_MOVING,
    "temperature": TEMPERATURE[DEPLOYED_NAME], "open_threshold": OPEN_THRESHOLD,
    "menu_threshold": MENU_THRESHOLD, "menu_size": MENU_SIZE, "max_tokens": MAX_TOKENS_BERT,
}
with open(os.path.join(DEPLOY_DIR, "routing.json"), "w") as handle:
    json.dump(routing, handle, indent=2)
if DEPLOYED_NAME in FINETUNED:
    model, local_tokenizer = FINETUNED[DEPLOYED_NAME]
    copy.deepcopy(model).to("cpu").half().save_pretrained(DEPLOY_DIR)
    local_tokenizer.save_pretrained(DEPLOY_DIR)
print(f"Saved to {DEPLOY_DIR}: {sorted(os.listdir(DEPLOY_DIR))}")

8. Takeaways¶

  • Deploy fine-tuned DistilBERT. It reaches 99.2% test accuracy (macro F1 0.992). The keyword rule reaches 73.3%, and always predicting the most common intent reaches 12.5%.

  • The benchmarks lose money; DistilBERT makes it. The keyword rule sends 8.8% of supported test commands into the wrong money workflow and loses about $807k a year. Behind the gate, DistilBERT makes **no wrong routes on supported commands**. That is worth about $139k a year at 5,000 commands a day, and the choice holds for any cost of a money error from $0.50 to $50.

  • Managerial decision: three tiers.

    • Calibrated confidence ≥ 0.963: open the workflow.
    • 0.45–0.963: show a menu with the 3 most likely intents plus "something else".
    • < 0.45: "we did not understand".

    On test, 93.3% open directly and the remaining 6.7% get a menu that always contains the right intent. There are no fallbacks and no wrong routes, and value rises to about $152k a year.

  • Weak spot: out-of-scope requests. 6.7% still open a workflow (12% without the menu), mostly HELP_SUPPORT and never a money flow.

  • Caveats.

    • The test set is small (240 + 150 commands).
    • Validation accuracy (0.925) is the conservative figure.
    • The menu and error prices are assumptions for Sole to replace.
